To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the crystal structure of MtbFts2 reveals unexpected, G-protein-like conformational switchers that may be important for proper Z-ring assembly and function.

the structures of the MtbFtsGDP and MtbFtsGGTPgammaS complexes show an alpha-to-beta conformational switch analogous to the Switch I conformations of G-proteins, and that the presence of gamma-phosphate in GTP is directly coupled to this conformational change via the tubulin loop T3 (Switch II), which is also analogous to the conformational changes in G-proteins.

we report three crystal structures, of the Mycobacteria tuberculosis cell division protein, FtsZ, in the citrate, guanosine-5'-diphosphate (GDP), and guanosine-55'-triphosphate (GTPgammaS) complexes, determined at a resolution of 1.89 angstroms, 2.6 angstroms, and 2 angstroms, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural basis of the assembly of the Z-ring, a dynamic structure that forms in the middle of the cell, and that is essential to bacterial cell division.
the structure and function of the tubulin homologue FtsZ, which is the key protein in the bacterial cytokinetic apparatus.
the structure and mechanism of the bacterial cell division protein FTSZ.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the structure of MtbFtsz in the presence of GTPgammaS is a GTPase-like structure with a G-protein-like conformational switch, which is a new structural feature of FtsZ and tubulin.
the structure of FtsZ reveals an unprecedented G protein-like conformance switch.

the structures of the FtsZ protein in complex with GDP, citrate, or the nonhydrolyzable GTP analogue GTPgammaS, determined at high resolution, show that FtsZ is a G-protein-like dimer, and that the dimer interface contains an alpha-to-beta switch that may be involved in the assembly and function of the "Z-ring."
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the structure of MtbFts2 reveals unexpected, G-protein-like conformational changes that may play a role in the lateral assembly of Fts2 and the contraction of the Z-ring.
the FtsZ structures presented in this paper reveal a G-protein-like conformational switch, which is coupled to the GTP binding and GTPase activity.
we report the first crystal structures of a prokaryotic tubulin homologue and that the structures reveal an unexpected G protein-like confor-mational switching mechanism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the conformational changes that occur in tubulin and FtsZ are not unique.
FtsZ has a dimeric structure and a conformational switch, which is analogous to the conformational switch of tubulin, and which is coupled to the GTP binding and the GTP hydrolysis.
MtbFts2 is a dimer, which is different than the polymer that tubulin forms, and that the dimer interface of MtbFtsz is important for its function.
